newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - SGS-Thomson profit halved, keeps confidence.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - SGS-Thomson profit halved, keeps confidence.

text.p: European semiconductor group SGS-Thomson Microelectronics NV announced almost halved profits for the first six months of the year but said on Thursday it expected an improvement in margins in the fourth quarter.
The Franco-Italian group said first-half net income fell to $182.6 million from $351.1 million, while for the second quarter it dropped by about 48 percent to $92.1 million from $176.1 million.
The per-share figure for the second quarter was 66 cents, in line with the company's profit warning on June 5.
The shares fell on the Paris Bourse and closed 4.28 percent lower at 537 francs in a market that was down 0.98 percent.

"There were hopes that the company would have said it saw a rise in margins in the third quarter. It did not, it said the third quarter would be flat and it saw a rise in the fourth quarter," a broker said.
Goldman Sachs analyst Charles Elliott said the second-quarter profit was slightly better than expected but the full-year estimates might have to be reduced.
"I expected 62 cents, the market average was 65 cents and they delivered 66 cents," he told Reuters.

"The full-year consensus is $3.50 and that seems a little bit high now that recovery will start in the fourth quarter and not in the third," Elliott said. "But the next-year consensus of $5-plus is still very reasonable," he added.
Brokerage IMI Sigeco reduced its earnings-per-share forecast for SGS-Thomson to $3.71 from $3.78 but said the share was undervalued. SGS-Thomson reported earnings per share of $4.50 for 1996.

"While there may be disappointment in the further delay in the (chip market) recovery, evidence from Texas Instruments and Intel points to an upturn and SGS-Thomson has historically outpaced market growth," Denis Gross of IMI told clients.

SGS-Thomson shares have been rising from 440 francs on June 12 to 561 francs at the close on Wednesday. They added more than 10 percent in the last four trading days alone on better-than-expected results from other high-tech firms such as Intel Corp, Texas Instruments Inc and Motorola.
"The recovery in the semiconductor industry is progressing, albeit at a slower rate than we anticipated," said president and chief executive Pasquale Pistorio.

He said that the state of the market was becoming clearer, with a slightly higher order backlog for the third quarter compared to three months ago and a significant increase in the fourth quarter order book.
"Based upon this data, we expect to show progressive, sequential improvement in net revenues in the third quarter, with an acceleration in the fourth quarter of 1997," he said.
Net sales fell to $963.9 million from $1.04 billion in the second quarter and to $1.90 billion from $2.06 billion in the first half.

"We are increasing our level of investment in research and development and capital expenditure to support future growth," Pistorio said. Research and Development spending was increased to $151.5 million from $136 million in the second quarter.

"At the same time, however, we believe the current pricing environment is likely to continue into the third quarter, resulting in a gross margin for the third quarter in the same range of that of the second quarter. We expect the gross margin to improve in the fourth quarter," Pistorio said.

The gross margin -- net revenues minus cost of sales as a percentage of sales -- was 38.5 percent in the second quarter and 38.2 percent in the first quarter. It was 44.4 percent in the second quarter of 1996.
Pistorio told a news conference that the margin would return to a range of 40 to 42 percent in 1998. He said that in the fourth quarter of 1997, a margin of 40 percent was "desirable but difficult"
He told the news conference that on the medium and long-term he was "extremely confident" that SGS-Thomson would outperfom the markets it serves in terms of sales, profit and return on equity.

Pistorio said the company expected the world semiconductor market, in dollar terms, to grow between five and seven percent in 1997. This is in line with a May forecast by the company of seven percent but lower than the six to eight percent range forecast by Motorola on July 9.
Pistorio said that the dollar's strength was making the company more competitive and was reducing its cost base but the influence on the bottom line was very small.
